entities.summary:
Heinrich Isaac, a pivotal Netherlandish composer of the late 15th and early 16th centuries, stands as a towering figure in the transition from medieval polyphony to high Renaissance musical artistry. Though his exact birthplace in the Southern Netherlands remains unknown, his career trajectory spanned the most influential courts of Europe, from the burgeoning cultural hub of Florence under Lorenzo de' Medici to the imperial grandeur of Maximilian I's Habsburg court. Isaac's significance lies not only in his prolific output across sacred and secular genres but also in his crucial role in disseminating the sophisticated Franco-Flemish style, particularly into German-speaking lands, thereby shaping the musical landscape of Central Europe for generations.

Isaac's remarkable career began in the service of Lorenzo de' Medici in Florence from 1485 to 1492, where he composed a diverse repertoire including madrigals, *canzoni*, and instrumental pieces, absorbing Italianate influences. Following the Medici expulsion, he entered the employ of Emperor Maximilian I around 1497, serving as court composer in Vienna and Innsbruck until his death in 1517. This imperial patronage allowed Isaac to produce some of his most monumental works, including numerous masses, motets, and particularly the immense *Choralis Constantinus*, a cycle of motets for the Proper of the Mass encompassing the entire liturgical year—an unparalleled undertaking in its scope and ambition.
